questions.question: Mean intensity of solar radiation at Earth is 1.37 kW m^-2 and the Earth-Sun distance is 1.50 x 10^11 m. Show that the Sun's luminosity is about 4 x 10^26 W.
questions.answer: L = 4 pi d^2 I = 3.9 x 10^26 W, about 4 x 10^26 W
steps: Power spreads over a sphere centred on the Sun with radius equal to the Earth-Sun distance d.
Area of sphere: A = 4 pi d^2 = 4 pi (1.50 x 10^11 m)^2 = 2.83 x 10^23 m^2.
Intensity I is power per unit area, so total power L = I x A.

questions.question: The Sun loses mass because it radiates energy. Calculate the decrease in mass of the Sun over 1 year (1 year = 3.15 x 10^7 s), using luminosity 4 x 10^26 W.
questions.answer: Decrease in mass = 1.4 x 10^17 kg
steps: Energy radiated in one year: E = L t = 4 x 10^26 W x 3.15 x 10^7 s = 1.26 x 10^34 J.
Mass-energy equivalence: E = delta m c^2.
delta m = 1.4 x 10^17 kg.

questions.question: State where the stars Alnilam and Mintaka would be located on a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.
questions.answer: Top left of the HR diagram: very hot (blue) and very luminous stars, at the top end of or above the main sequence.
steps: On an HR diagram luminosity is on the vertical axis and surface temperature on the horizontal axis, with temperature increasing to the left.
Both stars are very hot (2.75 x 10^4 K and 3.00 x 10^4 K), so they lie at the hot (left) side.
Both are extremely luminous (5.37 x 10^5 and 9.00 x 10^4 times the Sun), so they lie near the top of the diagram.
So both are in the top-left corner (blue giants/supergiants), with Alnilam slightly higher than Mintaka.

questions.question: Calculate the wavelength at which peak radiation power occurs for Mintaka.
questions.answer: lambda_max = 9.66 x 10^-8 m (ultraviolet)
steps: Wien's law: lambda_max T = 2.898 x 10^-3 m K.
Mintaka: T = 3.00 x 10^4 K from the table.

questions.question: Calculate the radius of Alnilam.
questions.answer: Radius of Alnilam = 2.25 x 10^10 m
steps: Luminosity in watts: L = 5.37 x 10^5 x 3.85 x 10^26 W = 2.07 x 10^32 W.
Stefan-Boltzmann law: L = 4 pi R^2 sigma T^4, so R = sqrt(L / (4 pi sigma T^4)).

questions.question: Deduce which of these stars gives the lower intensity of radiation at the Earth.
questions.answer: Mintaka gives the lower intensity at the Earth (3.64 x 10^-8 W m^-2 compared with 4.56 x 10^-8 W m^-2 for Alnilam).
steps: Intensity at Earth I = L / (4 pi d^2) (inverse square law).
Mintaka's intensity is lower (about 80% of Alnilam's).

questions.question: Explain how a massive planet orbiting a star can cause a change in the wavelength of light received from the star.
questions.answer: The star moves in a small orbit about the star-planet centre of mass, so its line-of-sight velocity changes and spectral lines show a periodic Doppler shift.
steps: The planet and star both orbit their common centre of mass, so the star moves in a small orbit.
When the star moves towards Earth its light is blueshifted; when it moves away it is redshifted.
So the wavelengths of its spectral lines change periodically (Doppler effect).
The size of the shift depends on the star's velocity along the line of sight, which reveals the planet.

questions.question: A spectral line of wavelength 4.35 x 10^-7 m has a maximum shift of 3.19 x 10^-13 m. Calculate the maximum velocity of Gliese 876 away from the Earth.
steps: For speeds much less than c: delta lambda / lambda = v / c.
v = c x delta lambda / lambda = 3.00 x 10^8 x (3.19 x 10^-13 / 4.35 x 10^-7).
A redshift means the star is moving away from Earth at 220 m s^-1.

questions.question: Mark on the diagram the position of a star similar to the Sun.
questions.answer: A cross on the band of dots (the main sequence) level with the "1" mark on the luminosity axis, where L = 1 L_sun.
steps: The Sun is a main sequence star, so its cross must lie on the diagonal band of dots, not on a stray point.
The Sun's luminosity is 1 L_sun, so the cross is at the height of the "1" on the vertical axis.
Where the band crosses that level (about two thirds of the way along from the hot, upper-left end) is the position of a Sun-like star.

questions.question: Explain how the appearance of the HR diagram for a star cluster changes as the cluster gets older.
questions.answer: The main sequence turn-off moves down and to the right as the most massive stars leave the main sequence first and become red giants; old clusters show red giants and white dwarfs.
steps: In a young cluster all stars, including very luminous hot stars, are still on the main sequence.
The most massive stars use their hydrogen fuel fastest, so they have the shortest main sequence lifetime.
When hydrogen in the core runs out they leave the main sequence and expand into red giants (higher luminosity, lower temperature).
So the hot, luminous end of the main sequence is lost: the turn-off point moves down and to the right.
Older clusters therefore show red giants and, eventually, white dwarfs; only lower-mass main sequence stars remain.

questions.question: Using the two calcium absorption minima on the graph (laboratory wavelengths 393.4 nm and 396.9 nm), determine the velocity of Andromeda relative to the Earth.
questions.answer: v = 3.0 x 10^5 m s^-1 towards the Earth (blueshift)
steps: Read the minima on the graph (grid lines every 0.5 nm): 393.0 nm and 396.5 nm.
Both are shorter than the laboratory values 393.4 nm and 396.9 nm by 0.4 nm: a blueshift, so Andromeda is moving towards the Earth.
Doppler shift: v = c x (change in wavelength) / lambda = 3.00 x 10^8 x 0.4 / 393.4 = 3.05 x 10^5 m s^-1 (second line: 3.02 x 10^5 m s^-1).
Velocity of Andromeda relative to the Earth is about 3.0 x 10^5 m s^-1 (300 km s^-1) towards us.

questions.question: It is claimed that dust around a standard candle makes it appear farther away than it really is. Assess the validity of this claim.
questions.answer: Valid: dust dims the light, so the measured intensity is too low and the inverse-square method then gives too large a distance.
steps: The distance from a standard candle uses I = L / (4 pi d^2), with L known.
Dust absorbs or scatters light, so the observed intensity I is lower than without dust.
Solving for distance: d = sqrt(L / (4 pi I)), so a smaller I gives a larger d.
The claim is therefore valid, unless the dimming is corrected for (for example by using colour data).

questions.question: Explain what is meant by redshift.
questions.answer: An increase in the observed wavelength of light from a source that is moving away from the observer.
steps: Light from a receding galaxy is observed at a longer wavelength than it was emitted.
Spectral lines are shifted towards the red (longer wavelength, lower frequency) end of the spectrum.
This is the Doppler effect: motion away from the observer stretches the wavelength.
Redshift z = (observed wavelength - emitted wavelength) / emitted wavelength.

questions.question: Light from NGC 6052 has redshift z = 0.0158. With H0 = 1.62 x 10^-18 s^-1, calculate the distance of NGC 6052 from Earth.
steps: For small redshift the recession speed is v = z c.
Hubble's law: v = H0 d, so d = v / H0.

questions.question: Two colliding galaxies accelerate towards each other. Explain why the acceleration increases as time passes.
questions.answer: The galaxies get closer, so the gravitational force between them increases (inverse square law) and so does the acceleration.
steps: The galaxies attract each other gravitationally.
As time passes the separation between them decreases.
Gravitational force F = G M1 M2 / r^2 increases as r decreases.
A larger force gives a larger acceleration (F = ma).

questions.question: Describe how trigonometric parallax can be used to determine the distance to a nearby star.
questions.answer: Measure the star's apparent shift against distant background stars at two points six months apart; distance d = 1 AU / parallax angle.
steps: Observe a nearby star against distant background stars at one time of year.
Observe it again six months later, when Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit.
The star appears to shift; half the angle between the two directions is the parallax angle p.
For small angles d = (radius of Earth's orbit) / p, i.e. d = 1 AU / p.

questions.question: Explain how knowledge of the distances to distant galaxies has enabled astronomers to determine a value for the age of the universe.
questions.answer: Distances (standard candles) and recession velocities (redshift) give H0 from v = H0 d; the age of the universe is approximately 1/H0.
steps: Distances to distant galaxies are found using standard candles and the inverse square law.
Recession velocities are found from the redshift of spectral lines.
Hubble's law v = H0 d gives the Hubble constant H0 from the gradient of v against d.
If galaxies have moved apart at a constant rate, their age since the Big Bang is T = d / v = 1 / H0.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a standard candle? A: a star of known distance, B: a star of known intensity, C: a star of known luminosity, D: a star of known mass.
questions.answer: C: a star of known luminosity
steps: A standard candle is an object whose luminosity (total power output) is known.
Its distance is found by comparing this luminosity with its observed intensity: I = L / (4 pi d^2).
Known distance (A) or known intensity (B) alone does not make a standard candle.
Mass (D) is not related to its brightness, so C is correct.

questions.question: State what is meant by a standard candle.
questions.answer: An object whose luminosity (power output) is known.
steps: A standard candle is an astronomical object of known luminosity.
Its apparent intensity on Earth can therefore be used to find its distance.
Examples include Cepheid variables and some supernovae.
The luminosity is known from a property such as period or type.

questions.question: A detector of area 1.00 x 10^-4 m^2 receives 9.40 x 10^-23 J in one burst lasting 1.15 ms, from a source 4.60 x 10^24 m away. Show that the luminosity of the source is about 2 x 10^35 W.
steps: Intensity at the detector: I = E / (A t).
The power spreads over a sphere of area 4 pi d^2 = 4 pi (4.60 x 10^24 m)^2 = 2.66 x 10^50 m^2.

questions.question: The source luminosity is about 2 x 10^35 W and the Sun's luminosity is 3.8 x 10^26 W. Suggest why alien communication is unlikely to explain the bursts.
questions.answer: The source is about 5 x 10^8 times more luminous than the Sun, far more power than a signal needs, so a natural astrophysical source is more likely.
steps: The source emits about 500 million times the Sun's power, which no sensible signal would need.
Such a brief, intense burst is more consistent with a natural astrophysical process.
So a natural origin is much more likely than deliberate communication.

questions.question: Determine the surface temperature of the star from its graph of relative intensity against wavelength.
steps: Read the peak of the curve: lambda_max = 0.385 um = 3.85 x 10^-7 m (between 0.38 and 0.39 um).
Wien's law: lambda_max T = 2.898 x 10^-3 m K.

questions.question: Explain what can be concluded about the star from the shifts of its spectral lines compared with laboratory values, including a calculation.
questions.answer: The star is moving away from the Earth (redshift) at about 1.6 x 10^7 m s^-1 (about 0.05c).
steps: Read the lines (ticks every 20 nm): star lines at about 480 nm and 656 nm; laboratory lines at about 454 nm and 624 nm.
The star's lines are at longer wavelengths than the laboratory lines (redshift), so the star is receding from the Earth.
Fractional shifts: 26/454 = 0.057 and 32/624 = 0.051, mean about 0.054.
v = c x (change in wavelength) / lambda = 3.00 x 10^8 x 0.054 = 1.6 x 10^7 m s^-1, about 5% of the speed of light.
A speed this large means the star is very far away, in a distant galaxy that is moving away as the universe expands.

questions.question: State what is meant by a main sequence star.
questions.answer: A star fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, in stable equilibrium between gravity and radiation pressure.
steps: Main sequence stars fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores.
Outward radiation pressure balances the inward gravitational force (hydrostatic equilibrium).
On the HR diagram they lie along a diagonal band from hot, luminous to cool, dim stars.
The Sun is a main sequence star.

questions.question: Show that the current radius of the Sun is about 7.0 x 10^8 m, given L = 3.83 x 10^26 W and T = 5780 K.
steps: Black body radiation: L = 4 pi R^2 sigma T^4 (Stefan-Boltzmann law).

questions.question: As a red giant the Sun's radius is about 150 times its current radius and its luminosity about 1600 times. Show that lambda_max is about 1 x 10^-6 m.
questions.answer: lambda_max = 9.7 x 10^-7 m, about 1 x 10^-6 m (surface temperature about 2980 K)
steps: L = 4 pi R^2 sigma T^4, so L / L0 = (R / R0)^2 (T / T0)^4.
Wien's law: lambda_max = b / T = 2.90 x 10^-3 m K / 2980 K = 9.7 x 10^-7 m, about 1 x 10^-6 m.

questions.question: Comment on the value of lambda_max from part (ii) and the classification of the Sun as a red giant. Red light lies between 6.2 x 10^-7 m and 7.8 x 10^-7 m.
questions.answer: lambda_max = 9.7 x 10^-7 m lies beyond the red end of the visible spectrum (infrared), consistent with a cool red giant surface, so the classification is consistent.
steps: Red light spans 6.2 x 10^-7 m to 7.8 x 10^-7 m, so 9.7 x 10^-7 m is longer than red light (infrared).
Most of the peak emission is therefore infrared rather than visible.
A long peak wavelength means a low surface temperature (about 3000 K), typical of a red giant.
A cool star looks red, so the red giant classification is consistent with the value.

questions.question: Explain how the orbital period of a planet changes as the mass of the Sun decreases, assuming the orbital radius does not change.
questions.answer: The period increases: T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3 / (G M)), so T increases as M decreases.
steps: Gravity provides the centripetal force: G M m / r^2 = m (4 pi^2 / T^2) r.
This gives T^2 = 4 pi^2 r^3 / (G M), so T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3 / (G M)).
For fixed r, T is proportional to 1 / sqrt(M).
As M decreases, T increases: the planet takes longer to orbit.

questions.question: Which of the paths WY, XY, YW or YZ is part of a possible evolutionary path of a star on the HR diagram shown (stars W, X, Y, Z)?
questions.answer: D: Y -> Z
steps: Y is a main sequence star; when its core hydrogen is used up it expands and cools into a red giant, moving up and to the right to the giant branch where Z is.
A (W -> Y) and C (Y -> W) are wrong: a star stays at one place on the main sequence while it fuses hydrogen, and does not move along it.
B (X -> Y) is wrong: X is a white dwarf, an end stage, which cannot become a main sequence star.

questions.question: Which statement about stars in positions W, X, Y and Z on the HR diagram is correct?
questions.answer: D: Y has a lower surface temperature than X.
steps: The temperature axis is reversed (arrow points left): temperature increases to the left.
X is to the left of Y, so X is hotter than Y, which makes D correct.
A and C are wrong: W is much more luminous than Y on the main sequence, so W is more massive than Y.
B is wrong: W is to the left of Z, so W is hotter than Z.

questions.question: Vega has 5 times the luminosity of Altair and is 1.5 times as far from Earth. The ratio I_V / I_A is about: A 0.5, B 1.5, C 2, D 5.
steps: Intensity at Earth I = L / (4 pi d^2).
Answer C.

questions.question: Stars X and Y have the same surface temperature. X has a radius 25% larger than Y. Which is the ratio L_X / L_Y: A 1.0, B 1.3, C 1.6, D 2.0?
steps: Luminosity of a black body star: L = 4 pi R^2 sigma T^4.
Same temperature means L is proportional to R^2 only.
This is closest to 1.6, answer C.

questions.question: Which of the following is true of dark matter? A: absorbs all electromagnetic radiation, B: emits no electromagnetic radiation, C: exerts no gravitational force, D: is a form of anti-matter.
questions.answer: B: it emits no electromagnetic radiation
steps: Dark matter is detected only through its gravitational effects.
A is wrong: it is not seen to absorb light.
C is wrong: dark matter does exert gravitational force, which is how it is inferred.
D is wrong: dark matter is not anti-matter, so B is correct.

questions.question: A metal bar is heated and then allowed to cool. Which statement about its peak emission wavelength lambda_max is correct? A: decreases as it cools, B: increases as it cools, C: increases as it is heated, D: constant as it is heated.
questions.answer: B: lambda_max increases as the bar cools
steps: Wien's displacement law: lambda_max = b / T, with b constant.
As the bar cools its temperature T decreases.
So lambda_max increases, which is option B.
A is wrong; C and D are wrong because heating decreases lambda_max.

questions.question: Two stars X and Y behave as black bodies; graphs show intensity against wavelength for each. Which statement can be deduced about brightness and surface temperature?
questions.answer: A: Star X is brighter and has a higher surface temperature than star Y.
steps: X peaks at a shorter wavelength than Y; by Wien's law lambda_max T = constant, so X has the higher surface temperature.
The curve for X is higher at every wavelength, so X emits more power per unit area.
Both are viewed from the same distance, so X is the brighter star.

questions.question: Complete the table with letters A, B and C to indicate the point on the rotating Sun corresponding to each measured wavelength of the alpha line.
steps: The rotation arrow shows the near face moving from left to right, so the left edge A moves towards the Earth and the right edge B moves away.
A is approaching: blueshift, shortest wavelength 656.2757 nm.
B is receding: redshift, longest wavelength 656.2837 nm.
C is at the centre of the disc, moving across the line of sight, so its wavelength is unshifted: 656.2797 nm.

questions.question: Explain why there is a variation in the wavelength of light from different points on the Sun.
questions.answer: The Sun rotates, so one edge moves towards Earth (blueshift) and the other away (redshift); the Doppler shift differs across the disc.
steps: The Sun rotates about its axis, so different points on its surface move at different velocities.
Points moving towards Earth show blueshift (shorter wavelength).
Points moving away from Earth show redshift (longer wavelength).
The line-of-sight velocity sets the size of the shift (Doppler effect).

questions.question: Assess whether the wavelengths measured from the Sun are consistent with a rotation period of about 28 days (lab alpha line 656.2797 nm, Sun radius 7.0 x 10^8 m).
questions.answer: Consistent: the shifts give a rotation period of about 2.4 x 10^6 s = 28 days.
steps: Edge speed v = c x (change in wavelength) / lambda = 3.00 x 10^8 x 0.0040 / 656.2797 = 1.83 x 10^3 m s^-1.
T = 2.4 x 10^6 / 86 400 = 27.8 days, which matches about 28 days.

questions.question: Stars P and Q have approximately the same radius, and the surface temperature of P is twice that of Q. The ratio L_P / L_Q is approximately: A 2, B 4, C 8, D 16.
steps: For equal radii, L = 4 pi R^2 sigma T^4 means L is proportional to T^4.
= 16, option D.
This assumes the ratio is L_P / L_Q as defined in the question.

questions.question: Tau Ceti has surface temperature 5300 K and luminosity 0.55 L_sun. Which is correct: A main sequence star, B red dwarf star, C red giant star, D white dwarf star?
questions.answer: A: main sequence star
steps: A temperature of 5300 K is similar to the Sun's, so it is a cool-yellow star.
Its luminosity of 0.55 L_sun is typical of ordinary main sequence stars.
Red giants are much more luminous, and white dwarfs are very faint.
So Tau Ceti is a main sequence star, answer A.

questions.question: The initial value of the Hubble constant was smaller than the accepted value. Which statement is correct? A: universe bigger than thought, B: universe not as old as thought, C: universe older than thought, D: universe smaller than thought.
questions.answer: C: the universe is older than astronomers initially thought
steps: The age of the universe is approximately T = 1 / H0.
A smaller H0 gives a larger T than the value first calculated.
So the universe is older than first thought.
Answer C.

questions.question: The intensity of Sirius is 1.09 x 10^-7 W m^-2 and its luminosity is 8.94 x 10^27 W. Calculate its distance from the Earth.
steps: Intensity I = L / (4 pi d^2), so d = sqrt(L / (4 pi I)).

questions.question: The gradient of a graph of red shift against distance (metres) is 5.4 x 10^-27. Which expression gives the Hubble constant in s^-1?
steps: For nearby galaxies the redshift is z = v / c, and Hubble's law gives v = H0 d, so z = (H0 / c) d.
The gradient of z against d (in metres) is therefore H0 / c.
H0 = c x gradient = 3 x 10^8 x 5.4 x 10^-27 = 1.6 x 10^-18 s^-1, which is option D.

questions.question: Show that 72 km s^-1 Mpc^-1 is equivalent to a Hubble constant of about 2.3 x 10^-18 s^-1 (1 Mpc = 3.09 x 10^22 m).
steps: Convert the velocity: 72 km s^-1 = 7.2 x 10^4 m s^-1.
Convert the distance: 1 Mpc = 3.09 x 10^22 m.

questions.question: Using H0 = 2.3 x 10^-18 s^-1, determine a value for the age of the universe in years (1 year = 3.16 x 10^7 s).
questions.answer: Age of universe = 1.4 x 10^10 years
steps: The age of the universe is approximately T = 1 / H0.
Convert: 4.3 x 10^17 s / 3.16 x 10^7 s per year = 1.36 x 10^10 years.
So the age is about 1.4 x 10^10 years.

questions.question: In the 1950s astronomers found galaxies were twice as far away as previously thought. Explain how this changed the calculated age of the universe.
questions.answer: The calculated age of the universe doubles.
steps: H0 = v / d: the velocity is unchanged but the distance is doubled, so H0 is halved.
The age T = 1 / H0.
Halving H0 doubles the calculated age of the universe.
So the previous estimate of the age was too small by a factor of 2.

questions.question: Parallax can determine distances to stars with parallax angle larger than 2.4 x 10^-7 rad. Alpha Cephei is 4.6 x 10^17 m from Earth and the Earth-Sun distance is 1.5 x 10^11 m. Deduce whether parallax can determine its distance.
questions.answer: Parallax angle = 3.3 x 10^-7 rad, larger than 2.4 x 10^-7 rad, so parallax can determine its distance.
steps: Parallax angle p = (Earth-Sun distance) / (distance to star) for small angles.
3.3 x 10^-7 rad is larger than the limit of 2.4 x 10^-7 rad.
So the distance to Alpha Cephei can be determined by parallax.

questions.question: Cepheids are a type of standard candle. Describe how standard candles can be used to determine distances to stars.
questions.answer: Known luminosity and measured intensity give distance through I = L / (4 pi d^2).
steps: Identify the standard candle (for example a Cepheid) and find its luminosity L from a known property such as its period.
Measure the apparent intensity I of its radiation at Earth.
Use the inverse square law I = L / (4 pi d^2).
Rearrange to d = sqrt(L / (4 pi I)).

questions.question: Label the x-axis of the HR diagram, including approximate values.
questions.answer: x-axis labelled "Temperature / K" (or surface temperature), decreasing from left to right, e.g. about 40 000 K at the far left, about 6000 K near Z3 (the Sun) and about 3000 K at the far right.
steps: Label the horizontal axis with the quantity and unit: surface temperature / K.
The scale must run backwards: hottest on the left, coolest on the right.
Give approximate values: roughly 30 000 - 40 000 K at the left end and 2500 - 3000 K at the right end.
A mid value of about 6000 K should be near Z3, which is the Sun-like star; the scale is logarithmic, e.g. 40 000, 20 000, 10 000, 5000, 2500.

questions.question: Complete the table, matching one of the zones Z1 to Z5 with each description.
questions.answer: High mass hot stars: Z1. Low mass cool stars: Z5. Low mass hot stars: Z2.
steps: Z1 is at top left: very hot and very luminous, so high mass hot (blue) main sequence stars.
Z5 is at bottom right: cool and dim, so low mass cool stars (red dwarfs).
Z2 is at bottom left: hot but dim (small radius), so white dwarfs, which are low mass hot stars.
Z3 (Sun-like main sequence stars) and Z4 (red giants) are not used in the table.

questions.question: Explain how a star like the Sun evolves as it progresses from zone Z3 to its final position on the HR diagram.
questions.answer: Z3 (main sequence) -> red giant (Z4 region) -> white dwarf (Z2 region, bottom left).
steps: In Z3 the Sun is a main sequence star: hydrogen fuses to helium in the core and gravity is balanced by gas and radiation pressure (stable for about 10^10 years).
When core hydrogen runs out, the core contracts and heats up; hydrogen fuses in a shell round the core and the outer layers expand and cool.
The star moves up and to the right to the red giant region (Z4): luminosity much greater, surface temperature lower, radius much larger.
The core becomes hot enough for helium to fuse to carbon and oxygen.
When fusion stops, the outer layers are ejected as a planetary nebula and the core is left as a white dwarf.
The white dwarf is small, hot and dim, so it lies at the bottom left (Z2); it then cools and fades with no further fusion.

questions.question: A lamp contains 1.65 x 10^19 mercury atoms in a volume 1.50 x 10^-5 m^3 at pressure 4.25 x 10^4 Pa. Calculate the mean kinetic energy of the atoms.
questions.answer: Mean kinetic energy = 5.80 x 10^-20 J
steps: Ideal gas law: pV = N k T.
Mean kinetic energy per atom = (3/2) k T = (3/2)(pV / N).

questions.question: A spectral line of Chi Lupi has wavelength 576.933 nm; the equivalent lab line is 576.959 nm. A student concluded Chi Lupi moves towards Earth at about 1400 m s^-1. Deduce whether the conclusions are correct.
questions.answer: Direction correct (towards Earth, blueshift), but the speed is about 1.35 x 10^4 m s^-1, not 1400 m s^-1.
steps: The observed wavelength is shorter than the lab value (576.933 nm < 576.959 nm), so it is blueshifted: Chi Lupi moves towards Earth.
Wavelength change: delta lambda = 576.959 - 576.933 = 0.026 nm = 2.6 x 10^-11 m.
The student's direction is right but the speed is about 10 times too small.

questions.question: Chi Lupi has surface temperature twice the Sun's and radius three times the Sun's. State where it would be located on the HR diagram.
questions.answer: On the main sequence, up and to the left of the Sun: surface temperature about 1.2 x 10^4 K and luminosity about 144 L_sun.
steps: L is proportional to R^2 T^4, so L / L_sun = 3^2 x 2^4 = 144.
T = 2 x 6000 K = 12 000 K, so Chi Lupi is hotter than the Sun and lies to the left of it on the HR diagram.
With a luminosity of about 100 times the Sun, it lies well above the Sun, in the upper left part of the main sequence (a hot blue-white star).

questions.question: Explain how the expression for velocity v of a star at distance r from the galactic centre gives the variation of v with r shown in the graph.
questions.answer: Inside the dense central region M increases with r, so v rises; beyond it M is almost constant, so v is proportional to 1/sqrt(r) and falls.
steps: In v = sqrt(GM / r), M is the mass inside radius r.
Near the centre the stars are densely packed, so M grows quickly as r increases (for constant density M is proportional to r^3, so v is proportional to r): v rises steeply from zero to a maximum.
Outside the central region there are very few stars, so M barely increases and is approximately constant.
Then v is proportional to 1/sqrt(r), so v decreases as r increases, giving the curved fall towards zero.

questions.question: Suggest why the observed velocity varies as shown in the second graph.
questions.answer: There is unseen (dark) matter spread through and beyond the galaxy, so the mass inside radius r keeps increasing and v stays high.
steps: The observed v stays roughly constant at large r instead of falling like 1/sqrt(r).
In v = sqrt(GM / r) this needs M to keep increasing roughly in proportion to r, which is far more mass than the visible stars supply.
So the galaxy must contain extra mass that emits no light: dark matter, spread in a halo around the galaxy.

questions.question: Explain why astronomers cannot be sure that the universe is closed.
questions.answer: The total mass (density) of the universe is uncertain, because the amount of dark matter and the effect of dark energy are not known.
steps: A closed universe requires average density greater than the critical density.
The total density includes dark matter, which cannot all be observed directly.
The effect of dark energy on expansion is also not well known.
So current models cannot reliably predict whether the universe is closed.

questions.question: The parallax angle of Wolf 359 is 2.01 x 10^-6 rad. Calculate its distance from Earth in metres (mean Earth-Sun distance 1.50 x 10^11 m).
questions.answer: Distance = 7.46 x 10^16 m
steps: For small parallax angle p, d = (Earth-Sun distance) / p.
Units: m / rad = m, as expected.

questions.question: Explain why parallax measurements can only be used to determine the distances to a relatively small number of stars.
questions.answer: Parallax angles for distant stars are extremely small, too small to measure accurately.
steps: The parallax angle is inversely proportional to distance.
Most stars are so far away that their parallax angles are very small.
Such tiny angles cannot be measured accurately with available instruments.
So parallax can only be used for a small number of nearby stars.

questions.question: Show that the surface temperature of Wolf 359 is about 2700 K from its intensity-wavelength graph.
steps: Read the peak of the curve: lambda_max = 1.07 um = 1.07 x 10^-6 m (the peak lies just above 1.0 um).
Wien's law: lambda_max T = 2.898 x 10^-3 m K.

questions.question: Wolf 359 has radius 0.16 R_sun and surface temperature 2700 K. It is claimed its luminosity is less than 0.1% of L_sun. Deduce whether this claim is correct (R_sun = 6.96 x 10^8 m, L_sun = 3.83 x 10^26 W).
questions.answer: L = 4.7 x 10^23 W, about 0.12% of L_sun, so the claim is not correct.

questions.question: Procyon has luminosity 2.65 x 10^27 W. A website states it has twice the diameter of the Sun (Sun diameter 6.96 x 10^8 m). Assess the accuracy of this statement.
questions.answer: Not accurate: Procyon's diameter is about 3.1 x 10^9 m, roughly 4.4 times the Sun's diameter, not 2 times.
steps: Read the peak of the graph: lambda_max = 460 nm = 4.6 x 10^-7 m.
The website's figure of twice the Sun's diameter is too small by more than a factor of 2.

questions.question: A standard candle in M81 has luminosity 14 800 times the Sun's (L_sun = 3.83 x 10^26 W). Its intensity at the top of the atmosphere is 3.64 x 10^-17 W m^-2. Calculate the distance of M81 from Earth.
questions.answer: Distance = 1.11 x 10^23 m
steps: Inverse square law: I = L / (4 pi d^2), so d = sqrt(L / (4 pi I)).

questions.question: Show that the surface temperature of Gliese-876 is about 3000 K from its graph of intensity against frequency.
questions.answer: T = 3.1 x 10^3 K, about 3000 K
steps: Read the peak of the graph: f_max = 3.2 x 10^14 Hz.
Convert to wavelength: lambda_max = c / f = 3.00 x 10^8 / 3.2 x 10^14 = 9.4 x 10^-7 m.
This is about 3000 K.

questions.question: A red dwarf should have luminosity less than 10% of L_sun. Using T = 3000 K from part (a), radius 2.62 x 10^8 m and L_sun = 3.83 x 10^26 W, evaluate whether the temperature supports this statement.
questions.answer: L = 4.0 x 10^24 W, about 1% of L_sun, so the temperature supports the statement.
steps: L = 4 pi R^2 sigma T^4 with R = 2.62 x 10^8 m and T = 3000 K.
L = 8.63 x 10^17 x 4.59 x 10^6 = 4.0 x 10^24 W, so L / L_sun = 1.0%, which is less than 10%.

questions.question: Describe how astronomers determine the luminosity of a standard candle and use it to determine the distance to a nearby galaxy.
questions.answer: Find the luminosity from a known property (for example the Cepheid period-luminosity relation), then use the measured intensity and I = L / (4 pi d^2) to find the distance.
steps: Identify a standard candle (for example a Cepheid variable) in the nearby galaxy.
Determine its luminosity from a known property: for a Cepheid, measure the period and use the period-luminosity relation.
Calibrate such relationships using standard candles whose distances are known from parallax.
Measure the apparent intensity I of the standard candle at Earth.
Apply the inverse square law: d = sqrt(L / (4 pi I)).
The galaxy's distance is therefore found; the redshift then allows the Hubble constant to be checked.

questions.question: Which row of the table gives possible values for X and Y on the HR diagram temperature scale?
questions.answer: D: X = 12 000 K and Y = 3000 K
steps: On an HR diagram temperature decreases to the right, so X (left) is hotter than Y (right); this rules out A and B.
The temperature scale is logarithmic, so equal spacing means equal ratios: X / 6000 = 6000 / Y.
D fits: 12 000 / 6000 = 2 and 6000 / 3000 = 2. C (9000 and 3000) would only fit a linear scale.

questions.question: Which of the following does not have the base unit s^-1? A: angular velocity, B: frequency, C: redshift, D: rate of decay.
questions.answer: C: redshift
steps: Angular velocity has units rad s^-1, and radians are dimensionless, so it is s^-1.
Frequency has units Hz = s^-1.
Rate of decay has units s^-1 (becquerel).
Redshift is a ratio of wavelengths, which is dimensionless, so it does not have units of s^-1: answer C.

questions.question: The spectrum from a galaxy is observed to be redshifted. Which statement about the lines is correct? A: all lines are in the red part of the spectrum, B: all lines have longer wavelengths than expected, C: lines at the red end are most intense, D: light was emitted with longer wavelengths.
questions.answer: B: all the lines are observed to have longer wavelengths than expected
steps: Redshift means the source is receding, so every line shifts to longer wavelength.
A is wrong: the lines are spread over the spectrum, not all in the red.
C is irrelevant to the shift, and D is wrong because the emitted wavelength is the same.
So the answer is B.

questions.question: Sirius has about 16 times the luminosity of the other star and is twice as far from Earth. Which of the options gives the value of the intensity ratio?
steps: Intensity I = L / (4 pi d^2), so I is proportional to L / d^2.
I_S / I_alpha = (L_S / L_alpha) x (d_alpha / d_S)^2 = 16 x (1/2)^2 = 4.

questions.question: Current theory suggests the universe is expanding. Which is evidence to support this? A: galaxies rotating, B: dark matter detected, C: distant stars increasing in size, D: the further a galaxy is, the faster it recedes.
questions.answer: D: the further a galaxy is, the faster it recedes
steps: Hubble's law: recession speed increases with distance (v = H0 d).
This is the observed evidence for an expanding universe.
A and B do not describe expansion, and C is not observed.
So the answer is D.

questions.question: The luminosity axis of an HR diagram has a logarithmic scale. Which is the reason? A: stars have very large luminosities, B: range of luminosities is very large, C: range of distances is large, D: temperature axis is logarithmic.
questions.answer: B: the range of luminosities of stars is very large
steps: Star luminosities span many orders of magnitude.
A logarithmic scale compresses a very wide range onto a readable axis.
A and C do not explain the scale, and D is about a different axis.
So the answer is B.

questions.question: Radiation from Sirius has 3 times the intensity of radiation from Canopus and Canopus is 36 times as far from Earth as Sirius. Which option equals the luminosity ratio L_C / L_S?
steps: I = L / (4 pi d^2), so L = 4 pi d^2 I.
L_C / L_S = (d_C / d_S)^2 x (I_C / I_S) = 36^2 x (1/3), since I_C = I_S / 3.

questions.question: Radiation of wavelength 134 nm was emitted from GN-z11 with redshift z = 10.96. Calculate the wavelength lambda_0 when detected by the HST.
questions.answer: lambda_0 = 1.60 x 10^-6 m (about 1603 nm)
steps: Redshift: z = (lambda_0 - lambda_e) / lambda_e, so lambda_0 = lambda_e (1 + z).

questions.question: Using the graph of z against the distance light has travelled, determine the distance light from GN-z11 has travelled to reach Earth, in metres (1 year = 3.15 x 10^7 s).
questions.answer: Distance = 1.3 x 10^26 m (about 13.5 x 10^9 ly)
steps: Find z = 10.96 on the vertical (logarithmic) axis, just above the 10 line, and read across to the curve and down to the axis: about 13.5 x 10^9 ly.

questions.question: Explain why the James Webb Space Telescope, designed to operate in the infrared, will help study very distant galaxies.
questions.answer: Light from very distant galaxies is redshifted into the infrared, so an infrared telescope can detect it.
steps: The expansion of the universe stretches the wavelength of light from distant galaxies (cosmological redshift).
Visible or ultraviolet light emitted by very distant galaxies arrives at Earth as infrared.
An infrared telescope can therefore detect the redshifted light.
This allows observation of very distant galaxies that would not otherwise be seen.

questions.question: Describe what is meant by dark matter.
questions.answer: Matter that does not emit, absorb or reflect electromagnetic radiation, so it is detected only through its gravitational effects.
steps: Dark matter does not emit, absorb or reflect electromagnetic radiation.
So it cannot be seen with telescopes.
Its presence is inferred from its gravitational effects on galaxies and other matter.
It contributes to the total mass of the universe.

questions.question: The new neutrino-type dark matter particle has mass 4.8 x 10^8 GeV/c^2. Calculate its mass in kg.
questions.answer: Mass = 8.5 x 10^-19 kg
steps: Energy equivalent: E = 4.8 x 10^8 GeV = 4.8 x 10^8 x 1.60 x 10^-10 J = 7.68 x 10^-2 J.

questions.question: Explain how the existence of dark matter contributes to the uncertainty in the ultimate fate of the universe.
questions.answer: Its total amount is not known, so the average density relative to the critical density is uncertain, and the universe's fate (expand forever or recollapse) cannot be fixed.
steps: The fate of the universe depends on whether its average density is greater or less than the critical density.
Dark matter contributes a large part of the mass and therefore the density.
Its amount is not precisely known, so the total density is uncertain.
Without the total mass, it is not known whether the universe will recollapse or expand forever.

questions.question: The spectrum of Kapteyn's Star has a peak at lambda_max = 8.12 x 10^-7 m. Show that its surface temperature is about 3600 K.
steps: Wien's displacement law: lambda_max x T = b, with b = 2.90 x 10^-3 m K.
T = 3.57 x 10^3 K, which is about 3600 K.

questions.question: The planet is 2.55 x 10^10 m from the star; the Sun's intensity at Earth is IE = 1380 W m^-2; the star's radius is 2.03 x 10^8 m. Show that the intensity at the planet is about 0.4 IE.
questions.answer: I = 6.0 x 10^2 W m^-2, about 0.44 IE, so about 0.4 IE.
steps: Black body star: flux at distance d is I = sigma T^4 (R / d)^2.

questions.question: Humans cannot survive a gravitational field 4 times the Earth's surface value. Kapteyn-b has radius 1.02 x 10^7 m and density 6.44 x 10^3 kg m^-3. Deduce whether humans could survive its surface gravity.
questions.answer: g = 18 N kg^-1, about 1.9 times Earth's surface value, which is less than 4 x 9.81 = 39 N kg^-1, so humans could survive.
steps: Surface gravity g = G M / R^2 with M = (4/3) pi R^3 rho, so g = (4/3) pi G rho R.
g = 18.4 N kg^-1, about 1.9 times 9.81 N kg^-1.
The limit is 4 x 9.81 = 39 N kg^-1, and 18 < 39.
So humans could survive the surface gravity of Kapteyn-b.

questions.question: Describe how stellar parallax is used by astronomers.
questions.answer: Measure a nearby star's position against distant background stars six months apart; the parallax angle p gives distance d = 1 AU / p.
steps: Observe a nearby star against distant background stars at one time.
Observe it again six months later, when Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit.
The apparent shift gives the parallax angle p (half the angle between the two positions).
Use d = (1 AU) / p for small angles to calculate the distance.

questions.question: Suggest why Tycho Brahe was not able to detect any stellar parallax.
questions.answer: The parallax angles of distant stars were too small for his instruments to measure.
steps: Stellar parallax angles are extremely small for stars at great distances.
Brahe's instruments could not measure angles that small.
So no shift was detected, which does not prove the Earth is stationary.
The lack of detection was a limit of measurement.

questions.question: State what is meant by a standard candle.
questions.answer: An object whose luminosity is known.
steps: A standard candle is an object of known luminosity.
Its measured apparent intensity can therefore be used to find its distance.
Supernovae are used as standard candles.
This is the basis of the inverse square law method.

questions.question: Describe how standard candles can be used to determine the distance to nearby galaxies.
questions.answer: Know the luminosity of the standard candle, measure its apparent intensity, and use I = L / (4 pi d^2) to find the distance.
steps: Identify a standard candle (for example a Type Ia supernova) in the galaxy.
Its luminosity L is known from its type or period.
Measure its apparent intensity I at Earth.
Use d = sqrt(L / (4 pi I)).

questions.question: A website says M87 is 55 million light-years from Earth. Its absorption line is at 394.5 nm, the lab value is 393.4 nm, H0 = 1.62 x 10^-18 s^-1, and 1 year = 3.15 x 10^7 s. Assess the accuracy of the statement.
questions.answer: Distance = 5.5 x 10^7 light-years, consistent with 55 million light-years, so the statement is accurate.
steps: Redshift: z = delta lambda / lambda = (394.5 - 393.4) / 393.4 = 2.80 x 10^-3.
Recession speed v = z c = 2.80 x 10^-3 x 3.00 x 10^8 = 8.4 x 10^5 m s^-1.
d = 5.2 x 10^23 / 9.45 x 10^15 = 5.5 x 10^7 light-years, so the claim is accurate.

questions.question: A star is moving away from Earth. Which explains why its spectral lines have different wavelengths from the lab? A: star emits shorter wavelength, B: star emits longer wavelength, C: light arrives with shorter wavelength, D: light arrives with longer wavelength.
questions.answer: D: the light arrives at the Earth with a longer wavelength
steps: A receding source produces a redshift (Doppler effect).
The star's emitted wavelength is the same; the change happens during travel to Earth.
A and B are wrong because the emitted wavelength is unchanged by motion; C would be blueshift.
So the answer is D.

questions.question: Betelgeuse has luminosity 4.49 x 10^31 W and peak intensity at 850 nm. A website claims its radius is 1000 times the Sun's (T_sun = 5800 K, L_sun = 3.83 x 10^26 W). Assess the accuracy of this claim.
questions.answer: R is about 990 times R_sun, close to 1000, so the claim is accurate.
steps: Surface temperature from Wien's law: T = 2.90 x 10^-3 / 8.50 x 10^-7 m = 3410 K.
Sun radius: R_sun = sqrt(L_sun / (4 pi sigma T_sun^4)) = 6.9 x 10^8 m.
Betelgeuse: R = sqrt(L / (4 pi sigma T^4)) = sqrt(4.49 x 10^31 / (4 pi x 5.67 x 10^-8 x 3410^4)) = 6.8 x 10^11 m.
R / R_sun = 6.8 x 10^11 / 6.9 x 10^8 = 990, about 1000 times: the claim is accurate.

questions.question: Add the approximate positions of the Sun and Betelgeuse to the HR diagram of main sequence stars, marked with labelled crosses.
questions.answer: Sun: cross labelled S at T about 5800 K (between 10 000 and 5000, nearer 5000) on L = 1 L_sun. Betelgeuse: cross labelled B at T about 3400 K (between 5000 and 2500) at L about 1 x 10^5 L_sun, near the top of the diagram.
steps: Sun: L = 1 L_sun and T = 5800 K. On the logarithmic temperature scale, 5800 K lies between 10 000 K and 5000 K, close to the 5000 K mark, so the cross is on the main sequence level with "1".
Betelgeuse temperature: T = 2.898 x 10^-3 / 850 x 10^-9 = 3400 K, between the 5000 and 2500 marks (a little over half way from 5000 to 2500).
Betelgeuse luminosity: L / L_sun = 4.49 x 10^31 / 3.83 x 10^26 = 1.2 x 10^5, so just above 10^5 on the vertical axis (halfway between the 10^4 and 10^6 marks, near the top).
Betelgeuse is a red supergiant, so its cross is at the top right, far above the main-sequence stars plotted.

questions.question: State what is meant by a main sequence star.
questions.answer: A star that fuses hydrogen into helium in its core in stable equilibrium, lying on the main sequence band of the HR diagram.
steps: Main sequence stars fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores.
Radiation pressure balances gravity, giving a stable star.
On the HR diagram they form a diagonal band from hot, luminous to cool, dim stars.
The Sun is a main sequence star.

questions.question: A neutron star has rotation period 33.5 ms and diameter 20.5 km and emits ultraviolet radiation of wavelength 91.2 nm. Calculate the maximum and minimum wavelengths observed.
questions.answer: Maximum wavelength = 91.8 nm; minimum wavelength = 90.6 nm
steps: Equatorial radius r = 10.25 km = 1.025 x 10^4 m; speed v = 2 pi r / T.
Doppler shift for v much less than c: delta lambda = lambda v / c = 91.2 nm x 1.92 x 10^6 / 3.00 x 10^8 = 0.58 nm.
Side moving towards Earth is blueshifted: lambda_min = 91.2 - 0.58 = 90.6 nm.
Side moving away is redshifted: lambda_max = 91.2 + 0.58 = 91.8 nm.

questions.question: Add a scale to the horizontal axis of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram for the star cluster.
questions.answer: Temperature (K) scale decreasing from left to right and logarithmic, e.g. 40 000, 20 000, 10 000, 5000, 2500 at equal spacing.
steps: Hot stars are at the left of an HR diagram, so the scale must decrease from left to right.
The scale is logarithmic: equally spaced ticks with values that halve each time, e.g. 40 000, 20 000, 10 000, 5000 and 2500 K.
The hottest main sequence stars here are at about 40 000 K (left end) and the coolest at about 2500 K (right end).

questions.question: Explain how this HR diagram shows that the star cluster is not a young star cluster, referring to groups of stars and their positions.
questions.answer: The diagram contains red giants (cool, very luminous) and white dwarfs (hot, dim), which only exist after stars have left the main sequence, so the cluster must be old.
steps: There is a group of stars at the upper right (cool but very luminous): red giants/supergiants, which are stars that have used up the hydrogen in their cores.
There is a group of stars at the bottom left (hot but very dim): white dwarfs, the end point of stars like the Sun.
These stars take billions of years to form, and in a young cluster nearly all stars would still lie on the main sequence, so the cluster is not young.

questions.question: Describe how measurements of standard candle V1 could show that the Andromeda Nebula is not a nearby star cluster.
questions.answer: Measure V1's period and apparent intensity; the inverse-square law gives a distance far beyond our galaxy, so Andromeda is outside it.
steps: Measure the period of V1, a Cepheid, and use the period-luminosity relation to find its luminosity L.
Measure the apparent intensity I of V1 at Earth.
Use d = sqrt(L / (4 pi I)) to find its distance.
If d is much larger than the size of our galaxy, V1 and the nebula lie outside our galaxy.

questions.question: A hydrogen line on Earth has wavelength 410 nm. A star moving away at 2.5% of the speed of light emits the same line. What wavelength is observed? A: 400 nm, B: 410 nm, C: 420 nm, D: 430 nm.
questions.answer: C: 420 nm
steps: The star is receding at v = 0.025c.
Observed wavelength lambda = lambda_0 (1 + v / c) for small speeds.
Answer C.

questions.question: Star X has twice the parallax angle of Star Y. Which is correct? A: X is twice as far as Y, B: X is four times as far as Y, C: Y is twice as far as X, D: Y is four times as far as X.
questions.answer: C: the distance of Star Y is twice the distance of Star X
steps: Parallax distance d = 1 AU / p, so d is inversely proportional to p.
Star X has twice the parallax, so its distance is half that of Y.
Therefore Y is twice as far from Earth as X.
Answer C.

questions.question: Which two measurements related to a distant galaxy must be used to determine the Hubble constant? A: distance and mass, B: distance and recession velocity, C: luminosity and mass, D: luminosity and recession velocity.
questions.answer: B: distance from the Earth and recession velocity
steps: Hubble's law v = H0 d relates recession velocity v to distance d.
H0 = v / d therefore needs distance and recession velocity.
Mass and luminosity are not part of Hubble's law.
Answer B.

questions.question: Which would result in an open universe? A: density equal to critical density, B: density less than critical density, C: mass equal to critical mass, D: mass greater than critical mass.
questions.answer: B: the average density is less than the critical density
steps: The fate of the universe depends on average density compared with critical density.
An open universe has density less than the critical density and expands forever.
Equal to critical density gives a flat universe; greater density gives a closed universe.
Answer B.

questions.question: Show that the surface temperature of Ross-154 is about 3000 K from its graph of power against wavelength.
questions.answer: T = 3.4 x 10^3 K, which is about 3000 K to 1 significant figure.
steps: Read the peak of the curve: lambda_max = 850 nm = 8.5 x 10^-7 m.
Wien's law: lambda_max T = 2.898 x 10^-3 m K.

questions.question: A website states Ross-154 has luminosity less than 0.5% of L_sun. Radius 1.18 x 10^8 m, surface temperature about 3000 K, L_sun = 3.83 x 10^26 W. Evaluate whether the statement is correct.
questions.answer: L = 8.0 x 10^23 W, about 0.21% of L_sun, which is less than 0.5%, so the statement is correct.
steps: L = 4 pi R^2 sigma T^4 with R = 1.18 x 10^8 m and T = 3000 K.
L / L_sun = 8.0 x 10^23 / 3.83 x 10^26 = 0.21%, below 0.5%, so the statement is correct.

questions.question: An Earth-type planet orbits Ross-154 at radius 0.096 AU (1 AU = 1.50 x 10^11 m). Ross-154 has mass 3.38 x 10^29 kg. Calculate the time for one orbit.
questions.answer: Time for one orbit = 2.3 x 10^6 s (about 26 days)
steps: Gravity gives the centripetal force: G M / r^2 = 4 pi^2 r / T^2, so T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3 / (G M)).

questions.question: State how astronomers knew that galaxies were moving away from the Earth.
questions.answer: From the redshift of their spectral lines (lines shifted to longer wavelengths).
steps: Spectral lines from distant galaxies are observed at longer wavelengths than lab values.
This redshift is due to the Doppler effect for a receding source.
So the galaxies must be moving away from Earth.
Hubble and others measured this redshift for many galaxies.

questions.question: Assess the validity of Hubble's expression v = H0 d based on the data shown in his graph.
questions.answer: Broadly valid but only roughly: the data show a clear trend of v increasing with d, consistent with a straight line through the origin, but with a large scatter.
steps: v = H0 d predicts a straight line through the origin; the plotted best-fit line passes through (0, 0) and most points lie close to it, with v increasing as d increases.
However, several points are far from the line (about a factor of 2 above or below, at both small and large d), so the scatter is large and the proportionality is not tightly confirmed.
The data cover only a small range of distances and a few points, so the relationship is plausible but not proved; more data at greater distance would be needed.

questions.question: Which must be known to use stellar parallax? A: distance between the Earth and the Sun, B: intensity of radiation from the star, C: luminosity of the Sun, D: value of the Hubble constant.
questions.answer: A: distance between the Earth and the Sun
steps: Parallax angle p = (Earth-Sun distance) / (distance to star).
The Earth-Sun distance is the baseline that must be known.
Intensity, solar luminosity and the Hubble constant are not needed.
Answer A.

questions.question: The HR diagram shows four areas P, Q, R and S. Which is a possible evolutionary path for stars initially in area P?
questions.answer: B: P -> S -> Q
steps: P is the hot, luminous end of the main sequence. When its core hydrogen is used up the star expands and cools into a red giant (supergiant), which is area S (cool, luminous).
After fusion ends, the outer layers are lost and the core is left as a white dwarf, which is hot but dim: area Q.

A is wrong (a white dwarf does not become a giant). C and D are wrong because R is a lower, cooler part of the main sequence, and a star does not move down the main sequence or return to it from the giant stage.

questions.question: Which of the HR diagrams W, X, Y or Z represents the cluster in its final stage of evolution?
questions.answer: C: Y, as there are white dwarf stars but no red giants in the cluster.
steps: As a cluster ages, the most massive, luminous main sequence stars leave first, so the main sequence loses its upper part, then the stars become red giants, then white dwarfs.
In the final stage even the red giants have gone: only white dwarfs (hot, dim, bottom left) and the few cool, low-mass main sequence stars remain. That is diagram Y.
Z is a young cluster (full main sequence). X has a few red giants but no white dwarfs yet. W has both red giants and white dwarfs, so it is not yet at the final stage.

questions.question: Absorption lines in the spectrum of a star are shifted to higher frequencies than the same lines from a source on Earth. Which can be concluded? A: accelerating away, B: accelerating towards, C: moving away, D: moving towards.
questions.answer: D: the star is moving towards the Earth
steps: A shift to higher frequency (shorter wavelength) is a blueshift.
Blueshift means the source is moving towards the observer.
Frequency shift alone does not indicate acceleration, so A and B are not supported.
Answer D.

questions.question: Kruger A has peak wavelength 850 nm and Kruger B has 1500 nm. A website states that Kruger A's surface temperature is double Kruger B's. Assess whether this is accurate.
questions.answer: T_A / T_B = 1.8, not 2, so the website statement is not accurate.
steps: Wien's law: lambda_max x T = b, so T is inversely proportional to lambda_max.
T_A / T_B = lambda_B / lambda_A = 1500 nm / 850 nm = 1.76.
A ratio of about 1.8 is not 2.
Kruger A is about 1.8 times hotter, so the website is not accurate.

questions.question: Kruger B can be used as a standard candle. Describe how standard candles can be used to determine the distance to galaxies.
questions.answer: Know the luminosity of the standard candle, measure its apparent intensity, and use I = L / (4 pi d^2) to find the distance.
steps: Identify a standard candle (such as Kruger B) with known luminosity L.
Measure its apparent intensity I at Earth.
Use the inverse square law I = L / (4 pi d^2).
Rearrange to d = sqrt(L / (4 pi I)) to give the galaxy's distance.

questions.question: NGC 1357 moves away at 2.02 x 10^6 m s^-1 and is 8.70 x 10^23 m from Earth. Calculate a value for the age of the universe in years (1 year = 3.15 x 10^7 s).
questions.answer: Age of universe = 1.37 x 10^10 years
steps: Hubble's law v = H0 d, so H0 = v / d.
The age of the universe is T = 1 / H0 = d / v.

questions.question: Pluto orbits the Sun at mean radius 5.91 x 10^12 m. The Sun has radius 6.96 x 10^8 m and surface temperature 5800 K. Calculate the intensity of solar radiation incident on Pluto.
questions.answer: Intensity = 0.89 W m^-2
steps: Sun's flux at distance d: I = L / (4 pi d^2) = sigma T^4 (R / d)^2.

questions.question: Calculate the time in years for Pluto to make one orbit of the Sun (r = 5.91 x 10^12 m, M_sun = 1.99 x 10^30 kg, 1 year = 3.15 x 10^7 s).
questions.answer: Time for one orbit = 249 years (about 2.5 x 10^2 years)
steps: Centripetal balance: G M / r^2 = 4 pi^2 r / T^2, so T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3 / (G M)).
T = 7.84 x 10^9 s / 3.15 x 10^7 s per year = 249 years.

questions.question: A line from a lab source has frequency 6.173 x 10^14 Hz, and the same line from a distant galaxy has frequency 6.142 x 10^14 Hz. Deduce the motion of the galaxy and calculate its speed (question wording is incomplete in the text).
questions.answer: The galaxy is receding at about 1.5 x 10^6 m s^-1.
steps: Observed frequency is lower (6.142 < 6.173 x 10^14 Hz), so the wavelength is longer: a redshift, so the galaxy is moving away.
Fractional change: delta f / f = (6.173 - 6.142) / 6.173 = 5.02 x 10^-3.
The galaxy recedes at about 1.5 x 10^6 m s^-1.

questions.question: Describe a possible evolutionary path for stars originally in area P of the HR diagram, referring to the type of star at each stage.
questions.answer: P (main sequence star) -> S (red giant/supergiant) -> Q (white dwarf).
steps: In P the star is a hot, luminous main sequence star, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core.
When the core hydrogen is used up, the star expands and cools to become a red giant (or supergiant) in area S: cool but very luminous.
Fusion then ends, the outer layers are ejected and the core remains as a white dwarf in area Q: hot but dim.

questions.question: Which statement about stellar parallax is correct? A: measurements are made against more distant stars, B: only for distant stars, C: luminosity must be constant, D: parallax is greatest for the most distant stars.
questions.answer: A: measurements are made against more distant stars
steps: Parallax is the shift of a nearby star measured against much more distant background stars.
B is wrong: parallax works only for nearby stars.
C is irrelevant, and D is wrong because parallax is smallest for the most distant stars.
Answer A.

questions.question: Show that when 4 protons form a helium nucleus the energy released is about 4.3 x 10^-12 J.
steps: Mass of 4 protons = 4 x 1.0078 u = 4.0312 u.
This is about 4.3 x 10^-12 J.

questions.question: Assess the claim that it would take 9 x 10^9 years for 10% of the hydrogen in the Sun to be fused into helium, considering the rate of helium production (mass of hydrogen 1.39 x 10^30 kg, L_sun = 3.83 x 10^26 W).
questions.answer: Not accurate: the Sun would take about 7.4 x 10^9 years to fuse 10% of its hydrogen, so 9 x 10^9 years is about 20% too long.
steps: Number of fusion reactions per second = L / E = 3.83 x 10^26 / 4.27 x 10^-12 = 9.0 x 10^37 s^-1.
Each reaction uses 4 protons: 4 x 1.0078 u = 6.69 x 10^-27 kg, so hydrogen fused per second = 9.0 x 10^37 x 6.69 x 10^-27 = 6.0 x 10^11 kg s^-1.
Mass to be fused = 10% of 1.39 x 10^30 kg = 1.39 x 10^29 kg.
The claim of 9 x 10^9 years is about 22% longer than the calculated 7.4 x 10^9 years, so it is roughly the right order but not accurate.

questions.topic: Main Sequence To White Dwarf Fusion
questions.question: Explain how main sequence stars evolve into red giants and then white dwarfs, referring to the fusion processes occurring in the star.
questions.answer: Hydrogen fuses to helium on the main sequence; the core then burns helium in the red giant phase; the remnant carbon-oxygen core cools as a white dwarf once fusion stops.
steps: On the main sequence, hydrogen fuses to helium in the core, releasing energy that balances gravity.
When core hydrogen runs out, the core contracts and heats, and hydrogen fuses in a shell around it.
The outer layers expand and cool, forming a red giant with greater luminosity.
When the core is hot enough, helium fuses into carbon and oxygen.
When core helium is exhausted, the outer layers are ejected and the hot carbon-oxygen core remains.
This core is a white dwarf: it no longer fuses and gradually cools.

questions.question: Wolf 359 has surface temperature 2700 K and luminosity 0.001 L_sun. Which describes it? A: blue giant, B: red dwarf, C: red giant, D: white dwarf.
questions.answer: B: red dwarf star
steps: A surface temperature of 2700 K means the star is cool and red.
A luminosity of 0.001 L_sun means it is very faint, so it is small.
A cool, faint main sequence star is a red dwarf.
Answer B.

questions.question: Which can be used to determine the distance to a nearby star? A: Doppler shift, B: Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, C: Hubble's law, D: trigonometric parallax.
questions.answer: D: trigonometric parallax
steps: Trigonometric parallax measures the shift of a nearby star against background stars.
Doppler shift gives velocity, not distance.
The HR diagram gives luminosity and temperature; Hubble's law applies to distant galaxies.
Answer D.

questions.topic: Intensity Graphs Star X And Y
questions.question: The graphs show radiation intensity against wavelength for star X and star Y. Which statement about their surface temperatures is correct?
questions.answer: D: T_X > T_Y because the peak intensity for star X is at the higher frequency.
steps: On the graph star X peaks at a shorter wavelength than star Y, which means a higher frequency (f = c / lambda).
By Wien's law (lambda_max is proportional to 1/T) the star with the shorter peak wavelength has the higher surface temperature, so T_X > T_Y.
A and B conclude T_Y > T_X, which is wrong. C has the right conclusion but the wrong reason: the peak of X is at the higher frequency, not the lower.

questions.topic: Red Giant To White Dwarf Table
questions.question: Which row of the table gives the changes in density and surface temperature as a red giant evolves into a white dwarf?
questions.answer: D: density increases and surface temperature increases.
steps: A red giant is a huge, low-density star with a cool surface (about 3000 - 4000 K).
A white dwarf is the core left behind after the outer layers are lost: about Earth-sized but with a mass similar to the Sun, so its density is enormously greater.
A white dwarf is also very hot (above about 10 000 K) and so appears white/blue-white, so the surface temperature increases.

questions.topic: Intensity Graph Stars P And Q
questions.question: The graph shows intensity against wavelength for stars P and Q. Which could be deduced? A: luminosity P > Q, B: mass P > Q, C: radius P > Q, D: temperature P > Q.
questions.answer: D: Temperature of P > Temperature of Q
steps: The peak of P is at a shorter wavelength than the peak of Q, so by Wien's law P has the higher surface temperature.
The luminosity, mass and radius cannot be deduced: the graph gives the intensity received, which also depends on the distance of each star, and no distances or sizes are given.

questions.question: Kepler's law relates the orbital time T of a planet to its average distance r from the Sun. Show that the expression given holds, where M is the solar mass.
questions.answer: T^2 = 4 pi^2 r^3 / (G M), obtained by equating gravitational force and centripetal force.
steps: For a circular orbit the gravitational force provides the centripetal force: G M m / r^2 = m r omega^2.
The angular speed is omega = 2 pi / T, so G M m / r^2 = m r (2 pi / T)^2 = 4 pi^2 m r / T^2.
Cancel m and rearrange: T^2 = 4 pi^2 r^3 / (G M), where M is the mass of the Sun.

questions.question: Our galaxy has mass 8.0 x 10^11 solar masses. A star is 5.7 x 10^20 m from the centre. Show that its orbital period should be about 8 x 10^15 s (solar mass = 1.99 x 10^30 kg).
steps: T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3 / (G M)) with r = 5.7 x 10^20 m.

questions.question: The observed orbital period of the star is 6.0 x 10^7 s, which does not agree with the calculated value. Deduce what this tells us about our galaxy.
questions.answer: The observed period is much shorter than predicted, so the galaxy contains much more mass than the visible (luminous) matter suggests: there must be dark matter.
steps: From T^2 = 4 pi^2 r^3 / (G M), at a fixed radius T is proportional to 1 / sqrt(M).
The observed period is shorter than the predicted 8 x 10^15 s, so the mass inside the star's orbit is larger than the 8.0 x 10^11 solar masses estimated from the luminosity: M = 4 pi^2 r^3 / (G T^2).

Note: the printed period 6.0 x 10^7 s would give an absurd M of about 3 x 10^58 kg; if it is a misprint for 6.0 x 10^15 s, M = 3.0 x 10^42 kg (about 1.5 x 10^12 solar masses), roughly twice the luminous estimate.
The extra mass does not emit light, so our galaxy must contain a large amount of dark matter, probably spread in a halo around it.

questions.question: The star Eridani has intensity 1.05 x 10^-9 W m^-2 at a distance of 9.94 x 10^16 m and radius 5.12 x 10^8 m. Calculate its peak wavelength lambda_max.
questions.answer: lambda_max = 5.6 x 10^-7 m (about 564 nm)
steps: T^4 = L / (4 pi R^2 sigma), with R = 5.12 x 10^8 m.
Wien's law: lambda_max = 2.90 x 10^-3 m K / 5140 K = 5.6 x 10^-7 m.

questions.question: The star Eridani recedes at 1.55 x 10^4 m s^-1. A spectrometer of resolution 0.05 nm observes light of wavelength 480 nm. Deduce whether a change in wavelength can be detected.
questions.answer: The shift is about 0.025 nm, which is less than the 0.05 nm resolution, so it cannot be detected.
steps: Doppler shift: delta lambda = lambda v / c.
Resolution of 0.05 nm is larger than 0.025 nm, so the shift cannot be resolved.
The scientist could not detect the change.

questions.question: Epsilon Indi is a main sequence star. Which row of the table gives a possible surface temperature and luminosity?
questions.answer: B: 4700 K and 0.14 L_sun
steps: Main sequence stars lie on the diagonal band of the HR diagram: lower temperature goes with lower luminosity.
B (4700 K, 0.14 L_sun) is a cooler, dimmer star than the Sun, which fits the lower right of the main sequence.
A (cool but 140 L_sun) and C (1400 L_sun) are far too luminous for their temperatures: giants. D (10 000 K but 0.014 L_sun) is hot but dim: a white dwarf.

questions.question: Explain why the spectrum of radiation received from Arcturus is shifted compared with that from the Sun.
questions.answer: Arcturus is moving relative to the Sun, so its spectral lines are Doppler shifted.
steps: Light from a source moving relative to the observer has its wavelength changed (Doppler effect).
Arcturus's motion relative to the Sun shifts the wavelengths of its spectral lines.
If Arcturus moves away the lines shift to longer wavelengths; if it moves towards, to shorter.
The size of the shift gives its velocity along the line of sight.

questions.question: Determine the speed of Arcturus relative to the Sun from the spectra shown.
questions.answer: v = 5 x 10^4 m s^-1 (about 54 km s^-1), moving away from the Sun
steps: Read the deep absorption line positions (small grid squares are 0.05 nm): Sun 883.83 nm, Arcturus 883.99 nm.
Shift = 883.99 - 883.83 = 0.16 nm towards longer wavelength: a redshift, so Arcturus is receding from the Sun.
v = c x (change in wavelength) / lambda = 3.00 x 10^8 x 0.16 / 883.8 = 5.4 x 10^4 m s^-1.

questions.question: Describe how astronomers use the shifts in spectra from galaxies to determine their distances.
questions.answer: Redshift gives recession speed v = z c; with Hubble's law v = H0 d, the distance is d = v / H0.
steps: Measure the shift of spectral lines to find the redshift z = delta lambda / lambda.
For small z the recession velocity is v = z c.
Apply Hubble's law v = H0 d, so d = v / H0.
The Hubble constant is found from standard candles, so the distance can be calculated.

questions.question: Show that the luminosity of Sirius is about 9.7 x 10^27 W, given radius 1.18 x 10^9 m and surface temperature 9940 K.
steps: L = 4 pi R^2 sigma T^4 for a black body sphere.
This is about 25 times L_sun, consistent with a hot, large star.

questions.question: A teacher claims that, from Earth, Sirius appears twice as bright as Canopus. Assess the accuracy of this claim, given L_Sirius = 9.7 x 10^27 W (from part (a)), L_Canopus = 4.12 x 10^30 W, d_Sirius = 8.15 x 10^16 m and d_Canopus = 2.93 x 10^18 m.
questions.answer: The intensity ratio is about 3.0, so Sirius appears about 3 times brighter, and the claim is not accurate.
steps: Intensity I = L / (4 pi d^2).
Ratio = 1.16 x 10^-7 / 3.82 x 10^-8 = 3.0, so Sirius appears about 3 times brighter, not 2.

questions.question: Which row of the table correctly links a condition with the ultimate fate of the universe?
questions.answer: B: density of the universe greater than the critical density, so the universe eventually contracts.
steps: The fate of the universe depends on its average density compared with the critical density.
If the density is greater than the critical density, gravity is strong enough to halt the expansion, so the universe eventually contracts (a closed universe).

A is wrong: at the critical density the universe expands forever (at an ever-decreasing rate), it does not contract. C and D are wrong: the comparison is made with density, not mass, and a mass greater than the critical value would lead to contraction, not endless expansion.

questions.question: The Sun emits radiation with peak intensity at frequency 6.1 x 10^14 Hz. Show that its surface temperature is about 6000 K.
questions.answer: T = 5.9 x 10^3 K, about 6000 K
steps: Peak wavelength: lambda_max = c / f = 3.00 x 10^8 / 6.1 x 10^14 = 4.92 x 10^-7 m.
Wien's law: T = b / lambda_max = 2.90 x 10^-3 m K / 4.92 x 10^-7 m.

questions.question: Label the position of the Sun on the incomplete HR diagram with a cross and an S.
questions.answer: A cross labelled S on the L = 1 line (level with "1"), at T about 5800 K: between the 10 000 and 5000 marks, close to 5000.
steps: The Sun has L = 1 L_sun, so the cross is level with the "1" on the vertical axis.
Its surface temperature is about 5800 - 6000 K, which on this scale is between 10 000 K and 5000 K, slightly nearer 5000 K (roughly three-quarters of the way along from 10 000 towards 5000).
Label the cross with the letter S.

questions.question: Add to the HR diagram to indicate the areas where main sequence stars (A), red giant stars (B) and white dwarf stars (C) are located.
questions.answer: A: a diagonal band from top left to bottom right through the Sun. B: upper right (cool, luminous). C: lower left (hot, dim).
steps: A (main sequence): a diagonal band running from the top left (about 30 000 K, L about 10^5) down to the bottom right (about 3000 K, L about 10^-3), passing through the Sun at (about 5800 K, 1).
B (red giants): an area in the upper right, cooler than about 5000 K and much more luminous than the Sun (L about 10^2 - 10^4), above the main sequence.
C (white dwarfs): an area in the lower left, hot (about 10 000 - 30 000 K) but very dim (L about 10^-2 - 10^-4), below the main sequence.
Each area must be clearly separate and labelled with its letter.

questions.question: Explain the conditions that were required to bring about and maintain fusion in the core of the Sun.
questions.answer: A very high temperature (about 10^7 K) and high density to overcome electrostatic repulsion between protons, supplied by gravitational collapse and maintained in hydrostatic equilibrium.
steps: Protons are positively charged and repel each other electrostatically.
They need very high kinetic energy to get close enough for the strong force to act.
This requires a very high core temperature, of order 10^7 K, supplied by gravitational collapse.
High density and pressure in the core increase the rate of proton collisions.
Gravity is balanced by radiation pressure from the fusion energy, giving hydrostatic equilibrium that maintains the conditions.
The energy released keeps the core hot, so fusion is self-sustaining while hydrogen remains.

questions.question: Explain why electromagnetic radiation is only absorbed at some wavelengths by atoms in the Sun's outer regions.
questions.answer: Electrons occupy discrete energy levels, so only photons with energy equal to the level difference (hf = delta E) are absorbed.
steps: Electrons in atoms occupy discrete (quantised) energy levels.
A photon is absorbed only if its energy equals the difference between two levels: hf = delta E.
Since E = hc / lambda, only specific wavelengths are absorbed.
These wavelengths appear as dark absorption lines in the spectrum.

questions.question: The wavelength difference between opposite ends of the Sun's equator is 7.94 x 10^-3 nm for the 589 nm line. A website states the Sun rotates once every 27 days at its equator. Assess the accuracy of this statement (radius 6.96 x 10^8 m, 1 day = 8.64 x 10^4 s).
questions.answer: The calculated period is about 25 days, so the 27-day figure is about 8% too long and not accurate.
steps: Opposite limbs move in opposite directions, so the total wavelength difference is 2 lambda v / c.
T = 2.16 x 10^6 s / 8.64 x 10^4 s per day = 25 days, not 27 days.

questions.question: The argon in a bulb is at 290 K and 75% of atmospheric pressure (1.03 x 10^5 Pa). The bulb volume is 1.25 x 10^-4 m^3. Calculate the number of argon atoms in the bulb.
questions.answer: Number of argon atoms = 2.4 x 10^21
steps: Pressure p = 0.75 x 1.03 x 10^5 Pa = 7.73 x 10^4 Pa.
Ideal gas law: N = p V / (k T).
N = 2.4 x 10^21 atoms.

questions.question: While the bulb is on, the argon pressure is 83% of atmospheric pressure. The manufacturer states the gas temperature is about 60 C. Assess whether this is accurate.
questions.answer: T = 321 K, about 48 C, so the 60 C claim is not accurate.
steps: The volume and amount of gas are constant, so p / T is constant: p1 / T1 = p2 / T2.
60 C (333 K) is higher than this, so the manufacturer's statement is not accurate.

questions.question: While the bulb is on, radiation from the filament has peak wavelength 1100 nm. The surface area of the filament is 1.55 x 10^-5 m^2. Calculate the power output of the bulb, treating the filament as a black body.
questions.answer: Power output = 42 W
steps: Stefan-Boltzmann law: P = sigma A T^4.

questions.question: Suggest why the actual power output of the bulb may be lower than the calculated value.
questions.answer: The filament is not a perfect black body (emissivity less than 1) and loses energy to the gas by conduction and convection.
steps: The calculation assumes a perfect black body radiating at full efficiency.
A real filament has emissivity less than 1, so it radiates less than this.
Some energy is also lost by conduction and convection to the argon gas.
Hence the actual power output is lower.

questions.question: State what is meant by a standard candle.
questions.answer: An object of known luminosity (absolute power output).
steps: A standard candle is an astronomical object whose luminosity is known.
Its distance can be found by comparing this with its observed intensity.
Cepheid variable stars are used as standard candles.
The luminosity is linked to a measurable property such as period.

questions.question: Show that the mean luminosity of this Cepheid variable star is about 8 x 10^29 W from its graph of luminosity against time.
questions.answer: Mean luminosity = 2000 L_sun = 7.7 x 10^29 W, about 8 x 10^29 W.
steps: On the luminosity-time graph the peaks are at about 3.5, 8.5, 13.5 and 18.5 days, so the period of the Cepheid is 5.0 days.
On the period-mean luminosity graph (logarithmic axes) read the line at a period of 5.0 days: the mean luminosity is 2000 L_sun.
Mean luminosity = 2000 x 3.83 x 10^26 W = 7.7 x 10^29 W.
This is about 8 x 10^29 W.

questions.question: The mean intensity of the Cepheid viewed from Earth is 5.1 x 10^-4 W m^-2, and its mean luminosity is about 8 x 10^29 W. Determine its distance from Earth.
questions.answer: Distance = 1.1 x 10^16 m
steps: Inverse square law: d = sqrt(L / (4 pi I)).

questions.topic: Main Sequence To Red Giant Change
questions.question: Which row of the table gives the change in diameter and the change in surface temperature when a main sequence star evolves into a red giant?
questions.answer: C: the diameter increases and the surface temperature decreases.
steps: When the core hydrogen runs out, the outer layers of the star expand enormously, so the diameter increases.
The expanded surface is much cooler (red), so the surface temperature decreases while the luminosity goes up.

questions.question: The initial estimate of H0 was 1.5 x 10^-17 s^-1, giving an age T. The current estimate is 2.1 x 10^-18 s^-1. What is the age using this value? A: 0.14 T, B: 0.71 T, C: 1.4 T, D: 7.1 T.
steps: The age of the universe is T = 1 / H0, so T is inversely proportional to H0.
The new age is 7.1 T.
Answer D.

questions.question: Astronomers use trigonometric parallax to determine distances to stars. Which must they know? A: distance between the Sun and a nearby star, B: diameter of the Sun, C: distance between the Sun and the Earth, D: diameter of the Earth.
questions.answer: C: the distance between the Sun and the Earth
steps: Parallax distance d = (baseline) / parallax angle.
The baseline is the Earth-Sun distance (radius of Earth's orbit).
The diameter of the Sun or Earth is not needed.
Answer C.

questions.question: Explain why trigonometric parallax can only be used to determine the distance to objects that are relatively close to the Earth.
questions.answer: Parallax angles for distant objects become too small to measure accurately.
steps: The parallax angle p is the baseline divided by the distance, so p decreases as distance increases.
For distant objects p becomes very small.
Such small angles cannot be measured accurately with current instruments.
So only relatively nearby objects can be measured.

questions.question: State what is meant by a standard candle.
questions.answer: An object whose luminosity is known.
steps: A standard candle is an astronomical object of known luminosity.
Its apparent intensity can be measured on Earth.
The distance then follows from the inverse square law.
Cepheid variables are examples.

questions.question: Describe how the method of standard candles is used to determine the distance to a distant star cluster.
questions.answer: Identify a standard candle in the cluster, find its luminosity, measure its intensity, and use I = L / (4 pi d^2) to find the distance.
steps: Identify a standard candle (for example a Cepheid) in the star cluster.
Determine its luminosity from a known property such as its period.
Measure its apparent intensity I at Earth.
Use d = sqrt(L / (4 pi I)).

questions.question: The radiation emitted by Tau Ceti has maximum intensity at frequency 5.50 x 10^14 Hz. Show that its surface temperature is about 5300 K.
steps: Peak wavelength lambda_max = c / f = 3.00 x 10^8 / 5.50 x 10^14 = 5.45 x 10^-7 m.
Wien's law: T = b / lambda_max = 2.90 x 10^-3 m K / 5.45 x 10^-7 m.

questions.question: Calculate the average kinetic energy of gas atoms at the surface of Tau Ceti.
questions.answer: Average kinetic energy = 1.1 x 10^-19 J
steps: Mean translational kinetic energy of a gas atom: E_k = (3/2) k T.
This uses the surface temperature found in part (a)(i).

questions.question: Planet Aita is 8.05 x 10^10 m from Tau Ceti (radius 5.52 x 10^8 m). A scientist suggests Aita receives the same intensity from Tau Ceti as Earth receives from the Sun (1360 W m^-2). Evaluate this suggestion.
questions.answer: Aita receives about 2.1 x 10^3 W m^-2, about 1.5 times the Earth's value, so the suggestion is not accurate.
steps: Intensity from the star: I = sigma T^4 (R / d)^2.
Earth receives 1360 W m^-2, so Aita receives about 1.5 times as much: the suggestion is not accurate.

questions.question: Complete the nuclear equation for the alpha decay of plutonium-238.
steps: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, 4 2 He.
Mass number: 238 = 234 + 4.
Atomic number: 94 = 92 + 2.
